claims.text: Adding a small volume fraction of nanoscale Y2O3 will improve the radiation tolerance of a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Y2O3 addition will preserve the alloy's mechanical integrity.
Introducing Y2O3 by powder metallurgy is an engineering-practical processing route.
The intervention consists of introducing 1–2 vol% well-dispersed nanoscale Y2O3 particles by powder metallurgy.
The intervention will produce uniformly distributed Y2O3 nanoparticles both along grain boundaries and within grains.
Y2O3 nanoparticles act as sinks for radiation-generated vacancies and interstitials.
Capture of vacancies and interstitials by Y2O3 nanoparticles reduces radiation-induced defect clustering.
Capture of radiation-generated defects by Y2O3 nanoparticles reduces irradiation-induced swelling.
The oxide–matrix interfaces will be coherent.
Coherent oxide–matrix interfaces help preserve the alloy's load-bearing microstructure under irradiation.
Relative to the unmodified alloy, the Y2O3-doped alloy will have lower irradiation-induced defect density.
Relative to the unmodified alloy, the Y2O3-doped alloy will exhibit less irradiation-induced swelling.
The reduction in radiation-induced damage metrics will be greater than 10%.
The Y2O3-doped alloy will maintain tensile strength comparable to that of the unmodified alloy.
The Y2O3-doped alloy will maintain hardness comparable to that of the unmodified alloy.
The beneficial mechanism should operate under high-energy ion irradiation at elevated temperatures within the alloy's thermal-stability range.
The beneficial mechanism may cease to operate when oxide particles coarsen or oxide–matrix interfaces degrade at extreme dose or temperature.
Oxide-dispersion-strengthened materials in other alloy systems provide precedent for defect-sink behavior and retention of mechanical properties.
The optimal Y2O3 particle size and distribution and the precise quantitative benefit in a multi-principal-element alloy remain uncertain.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction of approximately greater than 10% in irradiation-induced defects and swelling, or deterioration of mechanical properties, would falsify the hypothesis.
